title: Query-Based Asymmetric Modeling with Decoupled Input-Output Rates for Speech Restoration
one_liner: Restore speech directly across mismatched sample rates by encoding only the frequency band that exists in the input and generating the missing output band through learned queries.
lead: Speech restoration often assumes the corrupted input and the clean output live at the same sampling rate, meaning the same number of audio measurements per second. Real systems do not always satisfy that assumption. A phone call may arrive at one rate, while the target output must be produced at another; noise removal, dereverberation, and bandwidth extension may all be needed at once. This paper defines that multi-rate setting explicitly and builds TF-Restormer for it. The main design choice is asymmetric processing: the model spends most of its capacity analyzing the frequency content that is actually present in the input, then uses learned extension queries to synthesize the missing high-frequency content in the output. That matters because the model no longer wastes computation on repeated resampling steps that only force the data into a matched-rate format.

problem.h2: Matched-rate speech restoration is too restrictive
paras: Many restoration models start by resampling the input so it has the same rate as the desired output. That simplifies the architecture, but it also forces every task into a common grid even when the observed recording never contained the high-frequency content that the output requires.

The result is wasted structure. The model treats analysis and synthesis as if they were symmetric, even though denoising observed content and inventing missing content are different jobs. The paper names this setting extended sampling-frequency independence, or xSFI, and asks for one model that can operate natively when input and output rates differ.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Encode only the frequency region that is observed in the input, then ask a lightweight decoder to generate the output-only bands through query-based cross-attention, which means the decoder sends learned requests into the encoded input and pulls back the parts that matter for each missing band.

panels.title: 1. The input has limited bandwidth
panels.viz_args: Noisy or low-rate speech contains only part of the target frequency range
panels.caption: The clean target may require information above the highest frequency present in the recording.

panels.title: 2. Old systems resample everything
panels.viz_args: Force input and output onto one common rate before restoration
panels.caption: Resampling makes shapes match, but it does not create missing speech detail.

panels.title: 3. TF-Restormer encodes the observed band
panels.caption: Most of the model's analysis focuses on the part of the signal that is actually measured.

panels.title: 4. Queries request the missing output band
panels.viz_args: Decoder queries pull relevant context from encoded observed bands
panels.caption: The decoder does not mirror the encoder; it asks for exactly the information needed to synthesize the absent frequencies.

panels.title: 5. One model handles many rate pairs
panels.caption: The restored waveform is clean and rate-correct without inserting separate resampling stages for each task.

steps.b: Read the degraded waveform at its native rate
steps.text: Keep the original sampling rate because the model should start from the signal that was truly observed rather than from a resampled version that adds no new evidence.

steps.b: Split the spectrum into observed and target-only bands
steps.text: Identify which frequency bands are present in the input and which extra bands must be generated for the output.

steps.b: Encode only the observed part deeply
steps.text: Use the encoder on the available bands because those bands contain the direct evidence about phonetics, speaker traits, noise, and reverberation.

steps.b: Decode missing bands with extension queries
steps.text: Issue learned queries for output bands that were not observed, then let cross-attention gather the most relevant context from the encoded input bands.

steps.b: Train with fidelity and perceptual objectives
steps.text: Use waveform and frequency-domain losses plus a discriminator so the restored speech matches both the target content and the target listening quality.

paras: The paper changes how input and output rates are related inside the model. Instead of forcing the same rate on both sides, it treats output-only frequency content as a separate synthesis target.

hidden.name: The unobserved high-frequency speech content required by the output rate
paras: When the output rate is higher than the input rate, the waveform must contain frequency content that the microphone never measured. That missing band is the central hidden quantity. It cannot be recovered by simple resampling because there is no direct observation of it.

The model therefore has to infer that content from context inside the observed band. Harmonic structure, phoneme identity, speaker timbre, and the shape of lower frequencies constrain what high-frequency details are plausible. Query-based decoding makes that hidden target explicit.

heat.caption: Observed low bands anchor the prediction about the missing band, while darker inferred cells mark output bands that must be synthesized from context rather than copied.

reads.html: The hard part is the speech detail that the input recording never captured but the output format still requires.
TF-Restormer treats high-band reconstruction as a query-conditioned prediction problem over missing output frequency regions.

mechanism.h2: Why asymmetric query-based decoding matches the task
paras: Restoration at mismatched rates has two different subproblems. The first is analysis of what is already present, which includes separating speech from noise and correcting reverberation. The second is synthesis of content that was never present in the observed waveform. A symmetric encoder-decoder spends similar capacity on both sides even though the evidence is concentrated in the input. TF-Restormer shifts most capacity to the encoder because the model needs a detailed analysis of the observed signal before it can guess the missing band.

The query mechanism then narrows the synthesis job. Each output band asks for the pieces of encoded context that matter to that band, so the decoder does not have to rebuild the whole signal from scratch. Band-partitioned cross-attention is useful because different output regions depend on different cues: fricatives need different evidence from voiced vowels, and dereverberation cues live in different time-frequency regions from bandwidth extension cues.

stages.s: Degraded speech at native input rate
Issue extension queries for target-only bands
Synthesize restored output at target rate
One model for denoising, dereverberation, and bandwidth extension across rate pairs

math.words: Train the model to match the clean target waveform, match its frequency content after taking logarithms of magnitude, and fool a discriminator that distinguishes restored speech from real clean speech.
math.equation: L_total = L_perceptual + lambda_spec L_logspec + lambda_adv L_adv
symbols: a loss that measures whether the restored speech sounds close to the clean target
a loss on the logarithm of the speech spectrum, meaning how energy is distributed across frequencies
the adversarial loss coming from the discriminator
the weight on the frequency-domain loss
the weight on the adversarial term

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the waveform loss is 0.18, the log-spectrum loss is 0.30, and the adversarial term is 0.05.
If the model uses lambda_spec = 2 and lambda_adv = 0.5, the total becomes 0.18 + 2 x 0.30 + 0.5 x 0.05.
A lower total means the output is closer to the clean target in waveform shape, in frequency content, and in realism judged by the discriminator.

math.note: The architecture is the main new element, but the mixed objective matters because generated high-frequency content can sound sharp in a frequency plot yet still sound unnatural to listeners.

charts.title: Matched-rate baseline with resampling
charts.note: A matched-rate pipeline spends work on resampling because the model cannot directly reason about different input and output rates.

charts.title: TF-Restormer xSFI model
charts.note: The unified model handles several restoration settings with one design because the decoder generates only the missing target content instead of mirroring the whole input path. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported direction.

items.b: The missing band may be too ambiguous.
items.html: If the input is extremely narrowband or heavily corrupted, the observed cues may not constrain the absent frequencies enough, so the synthesized band can sound plausible but still be wrong for the speaker or phoneme.

items.b: Rate combinations outside training can be awkward.
items.html: A model trained on a fixed menu of rate pairs may struggle when deployed on new combinations because the query decoder has learned band relationships from the training set.
The discriminator can encourage sharper outputs, but it can also push the model toward artifacts if the balance among losses is poorly tuned.
This approach is strongest when the observed band still contains enough phonetic and speaker information to anchor generation of the target-only frequencies.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Prepare clean speech at 16 kHz and generate degraded inputs at several lower rates with added noise and reverberation. Compare a matched-rate baseline that upsamples first against a query-based model that encodes the observed band and decodes missing bands directly.

Report waveform error, log-spectrum error, and a listening-oriented metric on each rate pair. The demo should also visualize which output frequency bands were observed and which were synthesized, because the main claim is about treating those two regions differently.
demo.closing: The demo must show that native multi-rate modeling works because the system separates analysis of observed content from generation of output-only content.
